header: For the Petitioners: Mr. Khursheed Khan, Advocate.
For Respondents: Mr. Ruhul Amin, Advocate.
body: SYED ARSHAD ALI, J.- Mst. Roaida Bibi and her two minor children, through the instant petition, have called into question the validity of the judgment/decree dated 23.09.2025, passed by the learned Appellate Court, whereby the appeal filed by the respondent against the order dated 16.09.2023, passed by the learned Trial Court, refusing to set aside the ex parte decree, was allowed.

2. Mst. Roaida Bibi and her two minor daughters filed a suit for recovery of dower, comprising two tolas of gold ornaments and the respondent’s share in his parental house, maintenance for herself and the minors, dowry articles, etc. The suit was contested by the respondent/defendant through a written statement, wherein he denied the assertions contained in the plaint. Along with the suit, the plaintiff also filed an application under Section 17-A of the West Pakistan Family Courts Act, 1964 (“the Act”), seeking interim maintenance for the minors. Subsequently, the plaint was amended to incorporate the respondent’s second marriage as an additional ground for dissolution of marriage. Several opportunities were afforded to the respondent to file his written statement as well as a reply to the application under Section 17-A of the Act for interim maintenance. However, the respondent/defendant subsequently filed an amended written statement along with a reply to the application under Section 17-A of the Act. On 19.12.2022, the learned Trial Court passed an interim order directing the respondent to pay maintenance to the minors at the rate of Rs. 6,500/- per month for each minor.

3. When the matter came up for hearing on 31.01.2023, the respondent/defendant and his counsel were absent from the proceedings; accordingly, ex parte proceedings were ordered against him. On the following date, i.e. 16.02.2023, when the case was fixed for ex parte evidence, the respondent/defendant appeared before the Court along with his counsel and requested that the ex parte proceedings be set aside. The said application was not opposed by the plaintiff; however, the respondent/defendant expressed his inability to pay the interim maintenance as directed by the previous order. Accordingly, a final opportunity was granted to him to pay the outstanding amount.

4. On 20.03.2023, the respondent/defendant made a partial payment of Rs. 20,000/- towards maintenance of the minor. On the following date, the defendant was not personally present before the Court, and only the clerk of his counsel was present. The Court accordingly directed him to pay the outstanding amount towards maintenance. On 20.05.2023, no one appeared on behalf of the respondent; consequently, the Court passed an order for payment of interim maintenance and, on 22.05.2023, struck off the defence of the respondent/defendant to the extent of the plaintiff's claim for maintenance.

5. On 21.06.2023, the respondent/defendant was once again proceeded against ex parte, as neither he nor his counsel was present before the Court. Resultantly, the plaintiff was directed to produce her evidence. On 26.07.2023, the plaintiff produced three witnesses, whereafter the case was fixed for arguments on 16.09.2023. On the said date, the respondent/defendant filed an application for setting aside the ex parte proceedings; however, he did not bother to pursue the said application. Consequently, on the same date, a decree was passed in favour of the plaintiffs and against the respondent/defendant.

6. It was on 11.11.2024, after a lapse of fourteen months, that the respondent/defendant filed an application for setting aside the ex parte decree dated 16.09.2023. Before the learned Trial Court, it was contended on behalf of the respondent/defendant that, as a copy of the decree had not been communicated to him in terms of subsection (7) of Section 9 of the Act, he was entitled to seek setting aside of the ex parte decree. The learned Trial Court, while observing that the application was barred by limitation, dismissed the same. However, the learned Appellate Court set aside the said order on two grounds: firstly, that an application had earlier been filed by the respondent for setting aside the ex parte proceedings, which had not been considered by the learned Trial Court; and secondly, that, in terms of subsection (7) of Section 9 of the Act, a copy of the judgment had not been sent to the respondent. Therefore, according to the learned Appellate Court, the period of limitation would commence from the date on which the said copy was sent by the Trial Court to the judgment-debtor. Nevertheless, it is noteworthy that the respondent had filed the said application for setting aside the ex parte proceedings only after his Computerized National Identity Card (“CNIC”) was blocked by the learned Trial Court on account of his non-appearance before the Court.

7. The learned counsel for the petitioners has contended that the order passed by the learned Appellate Court is legally flawed, as admittedly, the judgment-debtor/defendant had participated in the trial and thereafter intentionally absented himself from the proceedings; therefore, his subsequent application, filed after a lapse of fourteen months, was patently barred by limitation.

8. On the other hand, the learned counsel for the respondent has contended that the ex parte judgment and decree passed by the learned Trial Court was not legally sustainable, as the respondent had filed an application for setting aside the ex parte proceedings on the date when the learned Trial Court was about to pronounce the judgment. Therefore, it was incumbent upon the learned Trial Court to first decide the said application and thereafter proceed further in the matter. In support of this contention, he has placed reliance on Shafqat @ Shafaat v. The State (PLD 2019 Supreme Court 43), Muhammad Umer v. Muhammad Qasim and another (1991 SCMR 1232), and Abdul Wahid v. Amiran Bibi (2006 MLD 1631).

His next contention is that the application filed by the defendant/judgment-debtor for setting aside the ex parte decree was within the period of limitation prescribed under Section 9(6) of the Act, as the period of thirty days would commence from the date on which the respondent received the attested copy of the judgment in terms of subsection (7) of Section 9 of the Act. Therefore, according to the learned counsel, the application was filed within the prescribed period of limitation, and he accordingly supported the judgment passed by the learned Appellate Court. In support of this contention, he has placed reliance on Syed Agha Hussain Shah and others v. Mst. Deena Bibi and others (PLJ 2017 Peshawar 1) and Muhammad Jalil v. Mst. Nagina Bibi and others (PLJ 2023 Peshawar 44).
9. I have given anxious consideration to the submissions made by the learned counsel for the parties and have perused the available record.
10. Before adverting to the merits of the case, let us first examine Section 9 of the Act, which is the central provision requiring interpretation by this Court.

S. 9 (1) Written statement……………………… (5) If the defendant fails to appear on the date fixed by the Family Court for his appearance, then– (a) if it is proved that the summons or notice was duly served on the defendant, the Family Court may proceed ex parte;

Provided that where the Family Court has adjourned the hearing of the suit ex parte, and defendant at or before such hearing appears and assigns good cause for his previous non-appearance, he may, upon such terms as the Family Court directs, be heared in answer to the suit as if he had appeared on the day fixed for his appearance; and (b) if it is not proved that the defendant was duly served as provided in sub-section (4) of section 8, the Family Court shall issue fresh summons and notices to the defendant and cause the same to be served in the manner provided in clauses (b) and (c) of sub-section (1) of section 8.

(6) In any case in which a decree is passed ex parte against a defendant under this Act, he may apply within 1 [thirty days of the service of notice under sub-section (7) of the passing of the decree] to the Family Court by which the decree was passed for an order to set it aside, and if he satisfies the Family Court that he was not duly served, or that he was prevented by any sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was heard or called for hearing, the Family Court shall, after service of notice on the plaintiff, and on such terms as to costs as it deems fit, make an order for setting aside the decree as against him, and shall appoint a day for proceeding with the suit; Provided that where the decree is of such a nature that it cannot be set aside as against such defendant only, it may be set aside against all or any of the other defendants also.

(7) The notice of passing of the ex-parte decree referred to in sub-section (6) shall be sent to the defendant by the Family Court together with a certified copy of the decree within three days of the passing of the decree, through process server or by registered post, acknowledgement due, or through courier service or any other mode or manner as it may deem fit.
(8) Service of notice and its accompaniment in the manner provided in sub-section (7) shall be deemed to be due service of the notice and decree on the defendant.

11. Section 9 of the Act provides that, upon receipt of the summons, the defendant is required to file a written statement on the date fixed by the learned Trial Court in terms of clause (a) of subsection (1) of Section 9. The procedure for ex parte proceedings is prescribed under subsection (5) of Section 9, which provides that, if the defendant fails to appear before the Family Court on the date fixed for his appearance, the Family Court may proceed ex parte, provided that the summons have been duly served upon him.

12. Subsection (6) of Section 9 prescribes the period of limitation and the circumstances in which an ex parte decree may be set aside. Under this provision, an application for setting aside an ex parte decree may be filed within thirty days of the receipt of notice under subsection (7) regarding the passing of the decree. The applicant is required to satisfy the Family Court that either he was not duly served or that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was heard or called for hearing. If either of these conditions is fulfilled, the Family Court may set aside the ex parte decree.

13. Similarly, subsection (7) of Section 9 provides that notice of the passing of an ex parte decree, along with a certified copy of the decree, shall be sent to the defendant by the Family Court within three days of the passing of the decree, through a process server, registered post acknowledgment due, courier service, or any other mode that the Court may deem appropriate.

14. The learned Appellate Court proceeded on the premise that, since a copy of the decree had not been sent to the respondent in the manner prescribed under subsection (7), the period of thirty days would commence from the date on which he received the said decree. There is no cavil with the said proposition. However, the mere fact that an application for setting aside an ex parte decree has been filed within the prescribed period of limitation does not, by itself, entitle the applicant to have the decree set aside as a matter of right. The applicant must also satisfy the Family Court that he was either not duly served or was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing when the suit was heard or called for hearing. Unless either of these conditions is fulfilled, the Family Court is not bound to set aside the ex parte decree merely because the application was filed within the period of limitation.

15. I have perused the application filed for setting aside the ex parte decree. It does not disclose any reason that prevented the respondent from appearing before the Court on the date fixed for hearing. Rather, the respondent himself admits that, on the date of the judgment, he appeared before the Court and even filed an application for setting aside the ex parte proceedings. Admittedly, neither of the grounds warranting the setting aside of the ex parte decree was available to the respondent.

16. The second ground urged by the learned counsel for the respondent was that, since an application for setting aside the ex parte proceedings had been filed, it was incumbent upon the learned Trial Court to decide the said application before proceeding further with the matter. There is no cavil with the said submission. However, the respondent had filed an application for setting aside the ex parte proceedings on the date when the learned Trial Court was about to pronounce the judgment, but subsequently remained absent from the proceedings for fourteen months. This irregularity on the part of the learned Trial Court could have been considered by the learned Appellate Court only if the said judgment had been challenged on that specific ground. In my humble view, however, the respondent could not seek relief on this ground after remaining indolent for fourteen months following the judgment and filing the application only when his Computerized National Identity Card (CNIC) was blocked.

17. The record further reveals the contumacious conduct of the respondent. Firstly, he was directed to pay interim maintenance, but he failed to comply with the said direction, as a result of which his right of defence to the extent of the claim for maintenance was struck off. Neither did the respondent challenge the said order nor did he subsequently comply with it, except for making a payment of Rs. 20,000/-.

18. A perusal of the overall evidence clearly demonstrates that the respondent was not serious about contesting the case. The filing of such applications, in the circumstances discussed above, appears to have been intended merely to prolong the proceedings and gain time, which cannot be permitted at the expense of the plaintiff, a financially disadvantaged woman, and her two minor children. The respondent's conduct, viewed in its entirety, also disentitles him to any equitable relief.

19. In view of the foregoing, the exercise of jurisdiction by the learned Appellate Court was patently illegal. Consequently, the impugned judgment/decree dated 23.09.2025, passed by the learned Additional District Judge- XV, Peshawar, is not sustainable in law and is hereby set aside. As a consequence, the original judgment/decree dated 16.09.2023, passed by the learned Judge, Family Court-IV, Peshawar, stands restored. The executing Court shall proceed with the matter in accordance with law.
20. The writ petition is allowed accordingly.
